paper_title: HiFOR: Hierarchical Foresight with Action-Guided World Grounding for Vision-Language-Action Model

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated promising capabilities in robotic manipulation by integrating visual perception, language understanding, and action generation. Recent advances have further incorporated future prediction to enhance the understanding of environmental dynamics and task progression. However, existing methods often model short-term dynamics and long-term task objectives separately, while directly incorporating predicted futures into action policies without sufficiently considering their relevance to current action requirements. To address these limitations, we propose HiFOR, a hierarchical foresight framework with action-guided world retrieval. Specifically, Hierarchical Foresight Prediction jointly predicts short-term state evolution, semantic milestones, and final goal states through a Hierarchical Dependency Mask (HDM), establishing dependencies across temporal horizons. Building upon these predictions, Structure-Aware Latent World Modeling organizes future latent representations along the horizon, view, and spatial dimensions to facilitate fine-grained retrieval. Furthermore, Action-Guided Factorized World Retrieval adaptively retrieves relevant future information from the structured latent world based on evolving action representations during denoising, providing targeted guidance for action generation. Extensive experiments on two simulation benchmarks and six real-world robotic manipulation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

sections.content: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated promising capabilities in robotic manipulation by integrating visual perception, language understanding, and action generation. Recent advances have further incorporated future prediction to enhance the understanding of environmental dynamics and task progression. However, existing methods often model short-term dynamics and longterm task objectives separately, while directly incorporating predicted futures into action policies without sufficiently considering their relevance to current action requirements. To address these limitations, we propose HiFOR, hierarchical foresight framework with action-guided world retrieval. Specifically, Hierarchical Foresight Prediction jointly predicts short-term state evolution, semantic milestones, and final goal states through Hierarchical Dependency Mask (HDM), establishing dependencies across temporal horizons. Extensive experiments on two simulation benchmarks and six real-world robotic manipulation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. 1. Introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [16, 17, 26, 29, 34, 46, 56, 59] have achieved remarkable progress in robotic manipulation by integrating visual perception, language understanding, and action generation within unified endFigure 1. Comparison of Foresight VLA Models. (a) Existing methods typically adopt single-horizon foresight and directly feed predictions into VLA models without selective utilization. (b) In contrast, HiFOR combines multi-horizon foresight with actionguided retrieval of relevant future information. to-end framework. Benefiting from advances in largescale vision-language models and the growing availability of diverse robotic demonstrations, recent VLA models have demonstrated promising capabilities across wide range of manipulation tasks. As robotic manipulation tasks become increasingly complex, anticipating future environmental changes and task evolution becomes essential for effective action generation. To this end, recent studies have explored incorporating foresight capabilities into VLA models to enhance their understanding of environmental dynamics and task progression [19, 27, 43]. Existing approaches primarily predict future states or latent representations to model environmental dynamics [15, 27, 30, 52, 57], or generate future images and videos to anticipate visual scene evolution [5, 19, 33, 43, 53], thereby providing additional foresight information for action generation. Despite these advances, effectively translating future predictions into actionable guidance for complex robotic manipulation remains challenging. First, modeling shortterm world dynamics or long-term task objectives in isolation limits hierarchical coordination across temporal horizons. As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), many existing foresight-based VLA methods primarily focus on single prediction horizon. Short-term prediction methods [8, 21, 47, 58] emphasize near-future environmental changes and local motion dynamics, capturing fine-grained state evolution but often lacking explicit connections to subsequent task stages and ultimate goals. In contrast, longterm prediction methods [9, 28, 36, 53, 54] provide intermediate task guidance through semantic subtask planning or visual subgoal prediction, enabling the policy to anticipate key future task states. However, these methods often lack sufficient modeling of the continuous state transitions and motion dynamics required to achieve such objectives. Although both forms of foresight provide valuable information, modeling them independently makes it difficult to establish explicit dependencies among local state evolution, key semantic milestones, and final task objectives, thereby limiting the policys coherent understanding of task progression across temporal horizons. More importantly, directly incorporating predicted future information into action generation often overlooks its varying relevance to current action requirements. As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), many existing approaches [8, 9, 38, 47, 53, 54, 58] directly incorporate predicted future images or latent representations into action policies as additional conditioning signals, without sufficiently distinguishing the relevance of different predictions to current actions. However, future information across different prediction horizons, camera views, and spatial regions contributes differently to action generation, and its relevance dynamically evolves throughout task execution and the action generation process. Therefore, even with rich and complementary future predictions, selectively retrieving and utilizing information relevant to current action requirements remains essential for fully exploiting the decision-making potential of foresight. These observations motivate unified framework that establishes hierarchical dependencies across temporal horizons and adaptively retrieves and leverages relevant future information according to current action requirements. To address these challenges, we propose HiFOR, hierarchical foresight framework with action-guided world retrieval for robotic manipulation. As illustrated in Fig. 1(b), HiFOR integrates multi-horizon foresight prediction with action-guided selective retrieval, enabling future information across different temporal horizons to provide targeted guidance according to evolving action requirements. Specifically, ❶ we first introduce Hierarchical Foresight Prediction, which jointly predicts short-term state evolution, key semantic milestones, and final goal states. By incorporating Hierarchical Dependency Mask (HDM), the prediction module establishes asymmetric dependencies across temporal horizons, connecting local motion dynamics with intermediate task progression and long-term objectives. ❷ Building upon these predictions, we propose Structure-Aware Latent World Modeling, which organizes predicted future latent representations along the horizon, view, and spatial dimensions to construct structured latent world while preserving fine-grained structural information for subsequent selective retrieval. ❸ Furthermore, we develop Action-Guided Factorized World Retrieval, which leverages evolving action representations during denoising to perform factorized attention over the structured latent world. By adaptively evaluating the relevance of different prediction horizons, camera views, and spatial regions to current actions, the retrieved future information provides targeted guidance for action generation. Through these designs, HiFOR effectively integrates hierarchical future modeling with action-guided information retrieval, enabling foresight predictions to better support robotic manipulation. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: First, we propose hierarchical foresight prediction mechanism that jointly models short-term state evolution, key semantic milestones, and final goal states through hierarchical dependency modeling, establishing explicit connections between local world dynamics and long-term task objectives. Second, we develop an action-guided structured world retrieval mechanism that adaptively retrieves future information relevant to current action requirements from structured latent world organized along the horizon, view, and spatial dimensions through denoising-aware factorized attention. Third, we conduct extensive experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and six real-world robotic manipulation tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of HiFOR and further validating the contributions of its key components through comprehensive ablation studies. 2. Related Works 2.1. Vision-Language-Action Model Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models aim to integrate visual perception, language understanding, and action generation to develop general-purpose robotic policies capable of executing complex manipulation tasks. Based on their action representations and generation mechanisms, existing VLA models can be broadly categorized into two paradigms: discrete and continuous action generation. Discrete action generation methods [3, 4, 17, 23, 31, 44, 45, 48, 54] convert continuous actions into discrete tokens 2 or textual sequences, enabling autoregressive action prediction. In contrast, continuous action generation methods [2, 13, 16, 18, 22] typically employ specialized action prediction modules to directly generate continuous control signals, mainly adopting regression-based, diffusionbased, or flow-matching-based approaches. Specifically, regression-based methods [18, 42] directly learn mappings from observations to actions, while diffusion-based methods [12, 25, 40, 41] generate action sequences through iterative denoising. Flow-matching-based methods [2, 16, 32, 35, 37, 60] learn continuous vector field to transform samples from noise distribution into the target action distribution. Although these approaches have improved the action generation and generalization capabilities of VLA models, they primarily focus on action prediction itself, whereas accurate local action predictions do not necessarily guarantee successful completion of complex manipulation tasks. 2.2. Foresight Predication in VLA To overcome the limitations of local action prediction, recent studies have incorporated foresight prediction into VLA to anticipate future environmental changes and task progression, thereby guiding action generation. Based on how future information is represented, existing methods can be categorized into implicit and explicit foresight prediction. Implicit methods [15, 27, 30, 49, 52, 57] model environmental dynamics in state or latent feature spaces, leveraging predicted future representations to facilitate policy learning and action generation. In contrast, explicit methods [5, 7, 19, 33, 43, 53] generate future images or videos to anticipate visual scene evolution and potential action outcomes, supporting robotic planning and decision-making. Despite these advances, existing methods still face limitations in modeling and utilizing future information. First, predicting short-term dynamics and long-term task objectives in isolation overlooks dependencies across temporal horizons, limiting coherent modeling of task progression. Second, existing methods often directly incorporate predicted future information into action policies as additional conditioning signals, without adequately considering its varying relevance to current action requirements. 3. Method 3.1. Problem Formulation We formulate robotic manipulation with VLA models as language-conditioned sequential decision-making problem. At each timestep t, the policy receives multi-view visual observations Ot = {I v=1, language instruction L, and } the robot state st, and predicts future action chunk: H1 h=0 = πθ(Ot, L, st), At = {at+h} (1) where denotes the action horizon. Each action at = [x, y, z, θx, θy, θz, g] relative consists of 3 end-effector translation, rotation, and gripper control. 3.2. Overview The overall framework of our method is illustrated in Fig. 2. Given language instruction, multi-view visual observations, and the robot state, we first employ VLA backbone to encode the current multimodal context and generate action representations. We then introduce Hierarchical Foresight Prediction (3.4), which jointly predicts shortterm state evolution, intermediate semantic milestones, and final goal states through Hierarchical Dependency Mask (HDM), establishing dependencies across prediction horizons. Building upon these predictions, Structure-Aware Latent World Modeling (3.5) organizes the predicted future latent representations along the horizon, view, and spatial dimensions to construct structured latent world model. Furthermore, we propose Action-Guided Factorized World Retrieval (3.6), which selectively retrieves action-relevant future information from the structured latent world to guide subsequent action generation. Together, these components enable our method to model hierarchical future evolution and selectively leverage relevant future information for action decision-making. 3.3. Hierarchical Foresight Planning Dataset We construct hierarchical planning dataset from existing successful expert demonstrations without collecting additional robot trajectories. Instead of uniformly sampling future frames, we identify semantically meaningful milestones to capture key task progression across different temporal horizons, providing structured future supervision for VLA training. As illustrated in Fig. 3, we first employ Planning Agent to generate task-specific semantic template from the language instruction L, decomposing it into an ordered sequence of subgoals = {G1, G2, . . . , GK}. Each subgoal specifies semantic stage, an event type, and completion verification criterion. For example, Pick up the red mug and place it on the plate can be decomposed into ❶ grasp the mug, ❷ move it to the target region, and ❸ place it on the plate, with the number and types of milestones determined by the task. Given the semantic template, we automatically localize the completion timestamps of each subgoal in expert demonstrations. Specifically, candidate event boundaries are identified using gripper transitions, robot motion phases, and state information. For stable-state events, such as grasping and placement, we select the earliest frame where the target condition remains persistently satisfied, while dynamic events are localized based on motion or statetransition boundaries. Hierarchical Foresight Prediction Complex robotic manipulation requires not only anticipating near-future environmental changes and motion dynamics but also understanding intermediate task progression and final goals. However, short-term world prediction and longterm semantic guidance in existing VLA methods often lack effective coordination, limiting their ability to capture task evolution across temporal scales. To address this, we propose Hierarchical Foresight Prediction. To evaluate the robustness of our method under diverse simulated environments, we perform experiments on both LIBERO [24] and RoboTwin 2.0 [10]. For LIBERO [24], we report the average success rate over four task suites, including Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long, where each suite contains 10 tasks. Each task suite is evaluated with 500 rollouts to obtain reliable performance statistics. For RoboTwin 2.0 [10], we follow the Hard evaluation protocol and assess our method on 20 randomly selected tasks with 100 rollouts per task. The Hard setting introduces challenging domain randomizations, including variations in clutter, illumination, textures, and object heights. Implementation Details. All experiments are conducted on 8 H200 GPUs with global batch size of 512 (64 per GPU). Both LIBERO [24] and RoboTwin 2.0 [10] are trained end-to-end for 30000 optimization steps using AdamW. The learning rate is linearly warmed up to 5105 over the first 5000 steps and then kept constant for the remaining training. We apply gradient clipping with maximum norm of 1.0 and maintain an exponential moving average of the model parameters with decay rate of 0.999. Performance on RoboTwin 2.0 Benchmark. As shown in Table 1, HiFOR achieves the best overall performance on RoboTwin 2.0 under the Hard setting, reaching an average success rate of 49.40% across 20 tasks, outperforming π0.5 by 9.05%. Specifically, HiFOR improves the success rates on Blocks Ranking RGB and Place Cans Plasticbox from 29% and 40% to 46% and 63%, respectively. Moreover, on Move Playingcard and Stack Blocks Two, HiFOR achieves success rates of 54% and 45%, surpassing the baseline by 14% and 13%, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of HiFOR in improving performance across diverse and challenging robotic manipulation tasks. Performance on LIBERO Benchmark. As shown in Table 2, HiFOR achieves the best overall performance on LIBERO, with an average success rate of 98.3%. Specifit achieves the highest success rates of 99.4%, ically, 98.6% and 95.8% on LIBERO-Spatial, LIBERO-Goal and LIBERO-Long, respectively, while remaining highly competitive on other task suites. Compared with the π0.5 baseline, HiFOR improves the average success rate from 96.9% to 98.3%, with the largest gain of 3.4% on long-horizon tasks. These results demonstrate that HiFOR effectively enhances long-horizon task execution while maintaining strong performance across diverse manipulation tasks. Table 1. Evaluation on Real-World Training and Evaluation Setting. To evaluate the effectiveness of HiFOR in real-world robotic manipulation, we conduct experiments on Generalization Tasks and Longhorizon Tasks using an AgileX Piper 6-DoF single-arm manipulator. The robot is equipped with parallel-jaw gripper and two Intel RealSense D435i RGB cameras, providing wrist-mounted and third-person visual observations. For Generalization Tasks, we use 100 expert demonstrations per task for training, while Long-horizon Tasks use 200 demonstrations per task. All models are trained on 8 H200 GPUs and deployed on single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU for realworld evaluation. Both task categories are evaluated with 50 rollouts per task, with object positions randomly initialized in each rollout to assess robustness and generalization under varying initial conditions. Performance on Real-World Setup. To evaluate the effectiveness of HiFOR in real-world robotic manipulation, we conduct experiments on six tasks involving object grasping, placement, and stacking. As shown in Fig. 4, HiFOR consistently outperforms π0.5 across all tasks, achieving an average success rate of 81.7%, an improvement of 11.0% over π0.5. Notably, HiFOR achieves 16.0% improvement on the challenging block stacking task, demonstrating its effectiveness in complex real-world manipulation. 7 Method LIBERO Short Milestone Goal AWR Spatial Object Goal Long 92.4 93.4 94.2 95.0 95.8 98.2 98.4 99.0 98.8 99. 98.8 99.0 99.2 99.0 99.4 98.0 98.0 98.0 98.2 98.6 RoboTwin2.0 Avg. 40.35 44.15 45.60 46.95 49.40 4.3. Ablation Study Key Component Analysis. We evaluate the key components of HiFOR through ablation studies in Table 3. Introducing short-term foresight prediction improves the average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 from 40.35% to 44.15%, while incorporating milestone and goal predictions further increases it to 45.60% and 46.95%, respectively. Adding action-guided world retrieval (AWR) further raises the success rate to 49.40%, an additional gain of 2.45%. Consistent improvements are also observed on LIBERO, particularly LIBERO-Long, where the success rate increases from 92.4% to 95.8%. These results highlight the complementary benefits of hierarchical foresight prediction and action-guided retrieval in effectively leveraging future information for robotic manipulation. Different Short-horizon Prediction Length. We investigate the effect of different short-horizon prediction lengths on LIBERO, as illustrated in Fig. 5. Specifically, we evaluate prediction horizons of 5, 10, and 15 steps. The 5step horizon achieves success rates of 95.8% and 98.3% on LIBERO-Long and LIBERO-Avg, respectively. Notably, the policy updates its predictions every 5 execution steps on LIBERO, naturally aligning the 5-step prediction horizon with the action execution interval. This alignment enables short-term foresight to provide effective guidance within the current execution cycle, whereas longer prediction horizons extend beyond the next prediction update. Different Future Prediction Representations. We investigate the impact of different future prediction targets by comparing direct pixel-level prediction of future RGB images with semantic feature-based future prediction. As shown in Fig. 6, RGB-based prediction improves success rates Figure 4. Real-world evaluation results.We evaluate HIFOR against leading models on the Generalization and Long-horizon task suites. Our method further achieves 95.8% and 98.3%, outperforming RGB-based prediction by 1.6 and 0.6 percentage points, respectively. These results demonstrate the benefits of future-aware supervision and suggest that semantic feature-based prediction provides more effective guidance for action generation, particularly in long-horizon manipulation tasks. 4.4. Qualitative Analysis Hierarchical Spatiotemporal Attention Visualization. To investigate how our method utilizes structured future information, we visualize the hierarchical spatiotemporal attention at representative timesteps from three task stages. As shown in Fig. 7, during stove activation, the model primarily attends to the milestone horizon (60%), focusing on 8 Figure 7. The Visualization of Action-Guided Factorized World Retrieval Across Task Stages. the wrist view and stove control knob. During grasping, attention shifts toward the short-term horizon (52%), emphasizing local manipulation details from the wrist view. During final placement, the goal horizon receives the highest attention (53%), with the third-person view highlighting the target placement region. These results illustrate that our method adaptively retrieves task-relevant future information across temporal horizons, camera views, and spatial regions. 5. Conclusion In this paper, we propose HiFOR, hierarchical foresightguided framework for vision-language-action robotic manipulation. HiFOR employs Hierarchical Foresight Prediction to jointly predict short-term dynamics, intermediate semantic milestones, and final goal states, capturing dependencies across different prediction horiStructure-Aware Latent World Modeling further zons. organizes these predictions along the horizon, view, and spatial dimensions to construct structured latent world. Action-Guided Factorized World Retrieval then adaptively retrieves action-relevant future information to guide subsequent action generation. Extensive experiments on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0, together with real-world evaluations, demonstrate the effectiveness of HiFOR in improving robotic manipulation performance.
